content.thinking:
Since the style calls for that hand-painted, chunky heroic Blizzard look, I'll go with custom painted gradients rather than cel-shading, maybe adding a subtle glow to the eyes. I'm deciding to design from scratch rather than referencing existing samples, since the brief points me away from that.

For the wolf itself, I'm sketching proportions exaggerated in Warcraft style — oversized head, thick shoulders, big paws, heavy ruff — with a shoulder height around 0.85m and total length near 1.9m including tail. I'm adding character details like a scar across the muzzle, a notched ear, and a leather collar with iron studs and bone beads for a worn, battle-hardened look.

Setting up the skeleton...

Continuing down the front leg chain to elbow, wrist, and paw, keeping it a straight vertical column with scapula/forearm/pastern segments and paw facing forward.

That's too plantigrade — wolves need steeper angles. I should use four segments for the forelimb (upper arm, forearm, pastern, toes) with the pastern angled up toward the wrist and toes flat on the ground, bending the elbow backward and letting the carpus come slightly forward to keep the column mostly straight.

Given the complexity of IK for each limb, I'm leaning toward manually placing points for a stylized wolf rather than relying purely on inverse kinematics, then verifying lengths and bone orientation with a bones preview and test shot. I'm now setting up the shoulder root position and target toe-tip coordinates, with segment lengths roughly 0.30, 0.30, 0.15, and 0.11 for the front leg.

For the paw, I'm making it a chunky oversized blob with roughly 0.075 radius to match the stylized proportions, then working out the hind leg setup: hip root position, toe target, and femur/tibia/metatarsus/toe lengths of 0.34, 0.34, 0.22, and 0.11, checking that the vertical reach to the ground works with knee-forward and hock-back bend directions.

Now I'm clarifying the joint structure — hip, knee, hock, toe base, toe tip — and confirming only two inner bend joints (knee and hock) are needed since the toe base is fixed by the sole constraint, matching the same pattern as the front leg's shoulder-elbow-wrist chain. For the torso, I'm considering using a swept loft along the spine with varying radii to get a barrel-like body shape.

I want three separate sweeps: torso (hips through spine to shoulders), neck (chest to head), and tail (hips backward), each parented appropriately with the hips as root, blending radii smoothly where they overlap so the body reads as one continuous Warcraft-chunky silhouette with a deep chest and tucked waist.

Continuing the neck path up to the head joint, then setting the head's parent and forward-down orientation to match an alert wolf pose.

Next I'm defining jaw and ear joints under the head, then building the tail chain from the hips backward with four joints curving slightly downward to a length of roughly 0.4-0.5 meters.

I'm checking proportions against real wolf anatomy to validate my numbers—body length from rump to chest should land around 1.0-1.3 meters with shoulder height near 0.7-0.85, so I'm cross-checking my coordinates against those targets.

Realizing my head-body total is running too long, I'm scaling down the pelvis and chest positions, then re-positioning the hips, spine, neck, and head to tighten the overall length while keeping the head slightly exaggerated for stylized proportions.

I'm now adjusting the shoulder height and withers position since my initial values put the wolf too tall compared to real proportions — lowering the body centers and radii to get withers closer to natural height before moving on to the legs.

Resetting the spine coordinates: pelvis, mid-spine, chest, and withers points with slightly rising y-values toward the shoulders, while keeping chest center lower so the belly line sits near realistic elbow height.

I'm defining torso radii at several points along the spine (pelvis, loin tuck, ribcage, chest, shoulders) to shape the sweep, planning to combine a torso sweep with a separate neck sweep that starts inside the chest for smooth continuity.

For the skeleton, I'm thinking through how the hips root connects to the spine chain—since the root joint can't be part of a chain itself, I'll duplicate the first position so the spine chain's initial joint sits right at the hips, giving a zero-length starting bone that's still valid.

For the body shape, I'll sweep a single combined path that runs from tail through hips, spine, and neck, using a radius function that varies along the parameter to taper the body naturally.

For the head, I'm placing the skull slightly forward from the neck joint and extending the snout further out, putting the nose around z≈1.04 and height close to 1.0, aiming for an alert forward-down gaze typical of a wolf.

For the body, overall standing height with ears up lands around 1.1-1.3, matching real alert wolf proportions. I'm planning a thick neck ruff and heavy mane using layered fur tufts and jagged spike-like clumps for a stylized Warcraft look, distributing them across the shoulders, spine, cheeks, chest, legs, and tail to build that hand-painted, textured silhouette.

For the palette, I'm going with a cool slate gray-blue body, dark back, cream belly, and warm tan accents, plus amber glowing eyes, dark nose, bone claws, and ivory teeth. For gear, I'm adding a brown leather collar with brass studs, a hanging bone fang and feather charm, and a scarred eye with painted slash marks for a tribal, battle-worn feel.

Now I'm designing the coat painting function that blends grays using noise-based streaks, layers a darker saddle marking across the back using noise thresholds tied to surface normal and position, and adds lighter cream tones on the muzzle, cheeks, belly, and inner legs with tan on the outer forelegs.

I'm opting for smoothstep-based gradients instead of hard cel-shaded edges to keep the painterly, soft-shaded Warcraft look rather than toon-style zigzag fur edges, baking in gradient shading so the underside reads darker and the top reads lighter, plus adding tan coloring with a darker stripe accent on the front of the forelegs.

I want one shared coat function reused across all furry body parts, built from position and normal to define zones: a darker mask over the muzzle top, cream on the muzzle sides and lips, a dark ring around the eyes like goggles, a darker forehead, and cream-white cheeks, with the head zone roughly defined by distance from the head joint position. Writing paint blending logic...

Adding more shading rules...

Defining more facial zones...

I'm shifting shadow colors toward a blue-violet tint for lower-facing normals and adding dirt darkening near the ground, plus designing the fur tufts as jagged gradient blades that can be tinted by a color parameter.

Rather than painting each tuft with its own hue, I'll use a greyscale gradient texture (darker base, lighter tip) multiplied by the coat color at each card's root, giving a painterly shaded look without flat coloring. I'll vary tuft shapes with randomized selection and place card clusters at the neck ruff, chest bib, shoulders, spine mane, and cheeks with different sizes for each region.

Thinking through the total card budget, I estimate roughly 1500 cards across all regions, each a simple 4-triangle flat card bent into 8-16 triangles, keeping the total well under the 60k triangle budget.

Now I'm sketching the head geometry itself—an ellipsoid skull with a snout built via a loft or frustum shape along stations on the head bone, working in the head joint's local coordinate frame to orient everything correctly for a forward-facing head.

For the snout, I'm shaping a tapering frustum from the skull front to the nose tip, narrowing in width and height as it extends forward, considering whether a loft with multiple stations would give a smoother, more natural wolf-like taper.

Defining the sweep radii...

For teeth, I'm adding canine spikes on both upper and lower jaw, with the mouth kept mostly closed but posed so the canine tips peek past the lip for a subtle snarl effect, like a Warcraft-style wolf.

For the mouth interior, I'm adding a dark reddish gap between the jaws and a pink tongue slab inside the lower jaw.

Now I'm working on the ears -- big triangular, chunky Warcraft-style ears with hinge joints positioned at the skull top, tilted slightly outward and forward, extruded for thickness with a dark outer layer and cream inner fur.

Setting up ear orientation vectors...

Verifying orthogonality checks out, then sketching the ear outline shape with base width and a pointed tip in local coordinates.

For the ear, I'm adding a smaller cream inset for the inner ear plus fur tufts at the base. For the eyes, I'm planning flattened amber spheres with slit dark pupils and a painted highlight decal, slanted in true Warcraft style.

I'm positioning these eye decals on the skull surface, angling them outward and slightly forward with an almond shape that slants down toward the nose for a predatory look, mirrored for each side. For the nose, I'm using a dark purple-black flattened sphere at the snout tip with a tiny white highlight dot.

Now I'm adding small dark pit spheres for nostrils, thin cream whisker rods, and dark painted brows. I'm also sketching a scar decal with three diagonal pinkish slash lines across the left cheek and eye area, and planning a leather collar sweep around the neck with studs, a buckle, and a fang/bead pendant for a Warcraft-style look.

I need to position the collar so the fur ruff cards don't completely hide it — placing it low near the chest, filtering out ruff cards too close to the collar plane, and sizing the ruff cards to lie flat along the surface so the studs and buckle stay visible.

Maybe a chunkier leather collar with a lifted lip works better. I'll model the torso and neck as one continuous sweep along the hips-spine-neck bone chain, computing radii as a function of arc-length position with piecewise-interpolated keyframes for width and height at each point.

Mapping out torso thickness from rump through hips, loin, ribs, chest, and into the neck base, tapering toward the head while keeping extra thickness around the ruff area, and double-checking that the chest depth and spine curve stay visually consistent.

Adding the head joint with a forward pitch off the neck end, nose extending out to about 1.02 height — keeping the alert, head-up wolf posture in mind.

Checking overall proportions: ears around 1.28, withers at 0.89, total height roughly 1.3, which fits a large stylized wolf scaled slightly above real gray wolf size. Now moving on to the leg joints, parenting the front legs to the last spine joint and the hind legs to the hips, and starting to place the shoulder blade joint for that chunky, broad-shouldered look.

Working through the front leg segment lengths to reach a toe target below and forward of the shoulder, balancing humerus, radius, carpus, and pastern lengths against the actual vertical and horizontal drop needed, while planning to visually verify the rig with a bones render before trusting the IK. I'm also setting paw width and spacing for that oversized stylized paw look, then shifting to lay out the hind leg root and toe target similarly on the back half of the body.

For the hind leg I'm placing the toe tip slightly behind the hip rather than directly below it, matching realistic hind stance, and assigning femur, tibia, metatarsus, and toe lengths that sum to the needed vertical drop, with knee bending forward and hock bending backward. Then I'm setting up a five-point chain (hip, knee, hock, toe base, toe) so I can sweep varying radii along it, making the thigh thicker at the top and tapering down toward the foot.

Still writing radius keyframes...

I'll make each toe from a small sphere with a dark claw spike, skipping dewclaws, keeping smooth limb sweeps by default, and add fur cards for thigh "pants" and foreleg feathering plus a shoulder mass sphere.

For the shoulders and haunches, I'm placing scaled part-spheres at the scapula and hip positions, bone-anchored to the torso and hips, sized big for that Warcraft silhouette. Then I'm plotting a bushy tail as a sweep along a curved path from the hips down and back, with a radius profile that's thicker at the base, widens slightly mid-tail, and tapers to a point at the tip.

I'm darkening the tail tip with a near-black gradient band and setting up a four-span joint chain (tail1 through tail4) parented to the hips, plus brush-tuft cards wrapping around the tail for volume. Now I'm layering in Warcraft-style accessories onto the collar — studded cylinders, a metal buckle, a hanging leather strap with beads, and a bone fang pendant, considering whether to add a small tribal feather charm too.

For the accent colors, I'm settling on a rich reddish-brown leather collar with iron studs, bone-colored pendant, and two feathers (teal and red-orange) for a saturated pop against the muted gray wolf palette. I'm also defining the paw geometry now, placing toe spheres so the lowest points sit right at ground level for proper contact.

Now I'm working out the toe/digit rigging — deciding to give each of the four feet four separate toe joints (16 total, well within the joint budget), each positioned so the pad sits just above the ground with target paw height around 0.058.

I'll make each digit a separate joint parented to toeBase, aimed toward its own tip, using rods and capsules with claws for the geometry.

Working out joint counts, roughly 70 total, then placing digit positions off the toe base with a fanned pad of capsules angled outward from the foot center.

Setting up digit joints with aim direction toward the tip, chunkier Warcraft-style proportions, and adding dark bone-colored claw spikes angled forward-down at each toe tip.

For claw and nose colors, I'm settling on a dark worn-horn shade rather than pure black for better readability, keeping claws a flat separate color from the coat paint. Now I'm sketching the eye texture as an almond shape with the inner corner angled toward the nose, giving it that classic slanted wolf-eye look.

Writing SVG eye code...

I'm adding a dark brow ridge rod above the eye for a fierce, alert look, then working out black lip lines along the snout's underside and a dark nose bridge using position dot products relative to the head axis.

Defining head local frame coordinates...

Defining the color palette...

Adding dark saddle markings...

Still defining leg and paw shading...

Then I'm layering highlight and shadow tones based on surface normal direction, blending toward frosty and shadowed hues for that painterly lighting effect, plus adding subtle darker stroke-noise lines for a hand-painted Warcraft feel.

Now I'm sketching a fur-tuft card shape as an SVG gradient blade with jagged spikes, shaded dark at the base and light at the tip, to layer onto the torso silhouette for texture.

I'm then figuring out placement rules for these fur cards: tinting them by the coat color, and scattering ruff tufts around the neck and chest with specific density, size, and flow directions so they lean and bend naturally, before planning a similar scatter along the dorsal ridge for the back mane.

Along with that I'm mapping out the remaining placement zones -- flanks, haunches, tail, cheeks, and the backs of the legs -- each with its own density, card size, and flow direction so the fur reads correctly on each surface, then estimating total card and triangle counts to keep the mesh reasonably light.

For materials, I'm figuring each tinted card group gets baked into a shared atlas rather than individual materials, so tint likely needs to be stored as vertex color per card. I'm also planning the jaw as a separate rest-pose joint with a slight open angle, and working out the collar construction by cutting a loop around the neck surface near the second neck joint to get a sensible radius for the torso cut.

I'm figuring out the exact neck joint positions and orientation so the collar loop sits at the right point, then working through how the sweep function's radius parameters map to the loop's local frame—unsure whether the binormal runs along the neck axis or radially, so I'll need to check visually. Writing stud placement code...

Now I'm thinking through how to position the pendant so it hangs from the front of the collar, trying to locate a reference point on the front of the neck surface to anchor the ray cast.

For the pendant itself, I'm planning a small torus ring with a fang-shaped spike hanging below plus a couple of beads, connected by a simple chain of rods. Then I'm reconsidering leg joint naming conventions, thinking about whether to use shoulder/elbow/wrist/paw/paw-tip style names so the tip joint of each limb chain reads naturally as the hand or foot.

Working through the actual joint-to-segment mapping now: with five points along the leg (root, three intermediate joints, and the end), the four segments correspond to humerus, radius, metacarpal, and toe lengths, placing shoulder, elbow, wrist, and toe-base joints at each span boundary before the tip.

Since the sole segment stays flat, the toe-base position gets derived backward from the paw tip using the toe length, which then determines where the metacarpal angles down from the wrist at roughly a 45° digitigrade slant. I'm also noting the leg chain setup with its sweep radius function spanning the full path to the tip joint, plus rough part counts for the body sweeps.

Now I'm sketching out the implementation: importing math, path, and paint helpers, building a profile function for radius keyframes, and laying out the torso and neck spine points as a sequence of control coordinates to be joined with a catmull path before being split into joint chains.

I'm working out how to unify the body path so the spine and neck chains share one continuous catmull curve, sliced at the neck's starting point using closestT, then building the hip root joint and tail chain from additional path points.

For the legs, I'm writing a loop that mirrors left and right limbs, defining root and target positions plus bend directions so the elbow points backward and the wrist points forward, keeping each limb constrained to a vertical plane since the root and target share the same x-coordinate.

Still writing limb/chain setup...

Now I'm sizing the front leg sweep radii along its length — thicker at the shoulder (0.095), tapering through the elbow and wrist, then flaring slightly at the paw base (0.045) for that chunky stylized look.

For the paw, I'm placing a padded sphere at the base of the toes, scaled asymmetrically so its bottom sits near ground level, then laying out four toe digits as small capsules fanned sideways with the outer toes angled back and out slightly.

Each digit gets a dark claw spike projecting forward and slightly down from the tip, sized so it stays just above the floor. I'll mirror this whole paw structure for the hind legs, using the chain's toe-base joint as the parent for positioning the digits.

For the digit joints, I'm deciding whether to attach pads to the toe-base joint or the tip joint, leaning toward treating the tip joint as the paw itself with digits as children. I also need to narrow the leg radius near the toe since the pad geometry will cover that area, then move on to placing head details using local coordinate offsets, being careful that "left" means positive X in this model's convention.

For mirroring, I'm testing whether negating the left offset correctly flips the position for the opposite side, planning to verify visually. Then I'm working out the skull's center position and ellipsoid scale relative to the head, followed by figuring out how to sweep the muzzle shape from the skull front to the nose.

Still writing sweep geometry...

Now I'm checking the width proportions between the skull and the snout base, then setting up the jaw joint's position and aim direction relative to the head, and sketching the lower jaw sweep from its pivot toward the chin with a tapering radius.

I'm adjusting the lower jaw curve so its tip sits almost flush against the underside of the upper snout, giving a nearly-closed mouth pose, then starting to place the upper and lower canine teeth as small spikes projecting from the snout tip and jaw front.

Now I'm adding smaller incisors and a row of tiny cone teeth along each side of the upper jaw edge, estimating their positions against the snout's curvature, then placing the nose as a small flattened sphere just forward of center.

I'm also planning a thin pink ribbon-like tongue as a capsule sitting slightly below the jaw's top surface, mostly hidden when the mouth is closed, and figuring out ear placement as hinged joints positioned up and outward from the head bone, with darker outer ear coloring and a lighter edge tone.

Painting ear surfaces now: an outer rigid shell in gray-toned coat material with a beveled edge, plus a smaller inner cream/tan slab offset forward, and a conditional paint rule that darkens the ear tips near the top edge.

I also want a notch cut into the right ear's outline for asymmetry, and I'm planning thin tapered rod whiskers (about 4 per side, radius tapering from 0.004 to 0.001) swept outward from the muzzle. Beyond that I'm considering eyebrow ridge spikes, cheek tuft cards, and a scar decal placed over one eye on the viewer's left side.

Working through the scar placement, I'm thinking of three pinkish slashes with darker edges running from brow to cheek, positioned near the skull's forward/up coordinates close to the eye location, which risks z-fighting between the eye and scar decals so I need to lift one slightly or offset them to opposite sides of the face rather than overlapping directly on the same eye.

I'm also figuring out the mirroring logic for the eye decal — since the left eye drawn with its inner corner toward the nose should appear correctly in a front view, I need to apply a mirror flag whenever the side value is negative so the decal orientation flips appropriately for the opposite side of the face.

I want to add a subtle glow to the amber eyes to give them a fierce, luminous look, while letting the dark eyelid areas stay unaffected by the glow. Collar details will wait until the torso surface geometry is finished, then I'll apply a worn-leather grain texture to the collar material for a weathered effect.

Now I'm planning hanging accessories: a fang-bone pendant on a cord at the throat using a spike shape anchored to the collar, with an iron torus ring and rod connecting it, plus feather charms made from extruded leaf-shaped outlines with teal coloring hanging from a short cord on the collar's side.

I'm working through the orientation math for the feather outline, setting its axis directions so the shape hangs downward with its tip facing away from the attachment point, checking the cross product to confirm the feather's flat face is visible from front and back.

I'm now adding a cream-colored chest bib patch using a normal and position-based mask, blending it into the torso coat zone while being careful it doesn't bleed onto the forelegs.

Writing coat paint function...

Checking that upward-facing normals get fully darkened by the saddle blend, which makes sense since the saddle should cover the upper back and flanks like a real wolf's coat pattern.

Now I'm figuring out the belly shading - mixing in cream color on the underside using the normal's downward component so it covers the chin, tail, and leg undersides consistently, plus adding an inner-leg gate based on horizontal normal direction to lighten the inside of the legs.

Then I'm adding a darker stripe down the front of the forelegs gated by z-normal and vertical position, keeping the hind haunch lighter and tan on the outer side, and starting a head-region override that blends in a distinct head color based on a local z-offset and vertical gate.

Now I'm defining the head's color palette: a tan-brown muzzle top with a dark center stripe, cream-white cheeks and chin, gray on the forehead and skull, and beginning to mask out dark patches around each eye based on distance from the eye positions.

Finally I'm layering in overall lighting effects—adding frost highlights toward the top, blue-toned shadows underneath, and dirt tinting near the ground—then returning the blended color as the final pixel value.

I'm checking that the mix function handles color strings properly by parsing them through a cached map, then setting up the tail with a gradient blend between the coat color and a tail-tip color, plus a darker saddle stripe along the top. Now I'm generating SVG texture code for fur tufts...

Next I'm starting the full file structure, defining the wolf's metadata and beginning the quadruped builder with a hip joint positioned and oriented as the root of the spine chain.

I'm building the spine curve through a sequence of control points along the back, then slicing it into a spine chain and a neck chain, assigning parent joints and roles accordingly.

Now I'm placing the head joint at the end of the neck chain with a forward-tilted direction, then setting up the torso sweep using the hips, spine, and neck bones with a defined profile.

I'm estimating the parametric position along the body path where the neck begins by summing up segment lengths, so I can place radius keyframes accurately along the sweep.

Working through the radius keyframe sequence...

I'm also considering using more sides for a chunkier look near the shoulders, and thinking about layering sphere joints onto the shoulder sweep before moving to the limb sweeps where radius will be defined as a function along the leg chain.

For the fur, I'm scattering points across the torso surface and generating card-based tufts with randomized size, lean, bend, and flow direction, colored using the coat paint. I need to filter out the collar region near the neck by computing distance from the collar plane so the ruff cards don't overlap with the neckline.

Checking the tip position confirms it clears the back edge fine. I'll keep the collar near the base of the neck with the ruff extending slightly beyond it, then move on to assembling the full file including the paws, dirt details, and haunch spheres using the coat positioning approach.

For the sphere geometry, I'm deciding to apply scale directly to the geometry rather than through the part options for safety, then position each sphere using the standard offset system. I'm also considering whether to keep normals smooth for an organic hand-painted look versus faceting them for a deliberate low-poly feel, and leaning toward smooth shading since that matches the Warcraft-style aesthetic better, though some faceting could still work as part of the chunky look.

Now I'm working out the shoulder sphere placement relative to the torso width to make sure it bulges outward just enough for that chunky silhouette, then moving into the head construction—setting up local offset helpers off the head bone, placing the skull sphere, sketching rough coordinates for brow ridges, and starting to sweep out the snout shape.

Adding the nose, highlight, and lip details...

Now I'm setting up the jaw joint anchored near the mouth hinge, aiming toward the front of the snout, then sweeping the lower jaw shape forward with tapering radius points along its length.

I'm adding a small chin tuft and tongue rod bound to the jaw bone, then placing a dark inner-mouth rod spanning between the jaws to suggest the mouth cavity when open.

Still writing teeth placement...

Still placing teeth and ears...

Shaping the ear outline...

Working out the ear orientation vectors...

Checking the thickness math: inner piece centered at 0.009 with thickness 0.012 spans from 0.003 to 0.015, which protrudes past the outer face at 0.010 as intended.

I'll skip extra ear-rim cards for now, but I'm adding cheek ruff cards on the skull surface, filtering by normal direction and height to scatter small cards with a leaning angle and downward flow. Then I need to place the collar and pendant after the torso, and set up whiskers as curved segments radiating from near the snout base.

Each whisker sweeps outward and droops downward using a bezier-like curve with tapering radius and bone coloring, kept thin and numerous but limited to a manageable count. For the eyes, I need to define a skull part and build a face skin surface combining the skull and snout.

Now I'm adding dark brow paint above the eyes and cream tear marks below them within the coat. I'm also setting up claws and fur cards along the legs, then writing a paw function that takes joint positions from the limb sweep and builds the foot geometry, referencing the leg chain's tip joint for positioning.

Writing digit capsules...

Claws start at the capsule's rounded cap tip so their base sits just inside the cap, which works fine, and the hind digits follow the same pattern with dirt paint already applied to the paws. I'm skipping dewclaws, setting the limb bend parameters, and now moving on to write the full file before typechecking it.

For the preview I'll use scattered surface hits as cards, and for the dorsal mane ridge I'll place frames along the torso's dorsal line, filtering scatter points by upward-facing normals and narrow x-range near the spine, then render them as small leaning cards with a dark color.

Now I'm defining distinct card groups: a neck/shoulder ruff covering the front, flank cards lying flatter across the barrel with wider spacing, and starting on the rump cluster.

Then I continue mapping haunch/thigh sweeps using outward-back facing filters, tail cards, foreleg back feathering, cheek tufts, and elbow details reusing the feathering filter. Tallying everything gives roughly 900 cards and about 7k triangles with a two-segment bend, which feels manageable, and I confirm the tint reads correctly off the coat colour including shading at each card's root.

For materials, I'm consolidating fur tufts into a shared texture list and leaning toward one material per texture-tint combination rather than per-card, assuming paint reads as vertex colors on a shared mesh, which should keep the atlas size reasonable. Writing SVG code for the eye texture...

Next I'm sketching the scar texture as three slash marks in a small viewBox.

Still placing pendant geometry...

I realize I should pass a frame instead, since a frame placed at the hit point naturally orients the torus so its plane aligns with the surface normal.

Rather than fight with axis conventions, I'll explicitly bind the pendant to the neck joint so it moves rigidly with the neck, then approximate the position near the throat and adjust manually. I'm also starting to think about adding a bead cord next.

I'll skip the nylon detail for now and just write the code, planning to iterate with the preview afterward. For helper function typing, I'll use `ReturnType<typeof b.joint>` for the joint type.
